## Motivation

California's Assisted Living Waiver (ALW) is a Medi-Cal Home and Community-Based
Services program. It is intended to let eligible people receive supportive care
in an assisted-living setting instead of an institution. At the time this
dataset was produced, participating facilities were located in 15 of
California's 58 counties.

This dataset can be used to study how the program's licensed capacity is
distributed geographically. For example, students can compare the number of
participating facilities with total capacity in each county, examine the highly
skewed distribution of facility sizes, and discuss what can and cannot be
inferred from administrative program data. Licensed capacity is a facility's
approved participant-enrollment-unit ceiling; it is not a count of current
vacancies.

California Care Compass assembled this analysis-ready release from the
[California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) ALW participating-facilities
GIS dataset](https://gis.dhcs.ca.gov/datasets/CADHCS::alw-assisted-living-facilities/about).
The [versioned open-data repository](https://github.com/asafichaki/california-alw-open-data)
includes the source links, methodology, machine-readable metadata, and the
standard-library Python script used to fetch and normalize the government data.
The [human-readable county tracker](https://californiacarecompass.com/data/california-alw-county-tracker-2026)
provides additional context and caveats.

## Data

Each row represents one DHCS participant-enrollment-unit/provider record. The
file contains 1,224 rows across 15 counties and a total licensed capacity of
39,065. All fields are complete except `address_2`, which is blank for 1,220
records because most facilities do not have a second address line. Blank values
are represented by empty CSV fields.

The `county` field uses the GIS-derived county name. Eleven source records have
a conflict between the source's free-text county field and mapped county name;
using the mapped field reproduces the published 15-county aggregate. Multiple
provider records can refer to the same street address, so rows should not be
interpreted as unique buildings without further entity resolution.


### Variable descriptions

| Variable | Description |
|----|-------------|
| `provider_number` | DHCS provider identifier. Treat as an identifier, not a numerical measurement. |
| `legal_name` | Legal name in the DHCS source. |
| `business_name` | Facility or doing-business-as name in the DHCS source. |
| `capacity_per_peu` | Approved participant-enrollment-unit capacity for the provider record; this is not live vacancy information. |
| `address` | Primary street-address line. |
| `address_2` | Secondary address line when supplied; blank for 1,220 records. |
| `city` | City name in the source. |
| `county` | GIS-derived California county name used for aggregation. |
| `zip_code` | ZIP or ZIP+4 code. Treat as text because it is a geographic identifier. |
| `phone_number` | Public facility telephone number in the DHCS source. |
| `latitude` | Facility latitude in decimal degrees. |
| `longitude` | Facility longitude in decimal degrees. |
| `source_access_date` | Date the DHCS source was accessed, in ISO 8601 format. |

## Questions

1. Summarize the distribution of `capacity_per_peu`. How do the mean, median,
   quantiles, and maximum differ, and which plots best reveal the distribution?
2. Group the records by county. Which counties have the most facilities, the
   greatest licensed capacity, and the highest median facility capacity? How
   sensitive are comparisons to the very different county populations?
3. What share of statewide capacity is located in the largest three counties?
   Use an appropriate visualization to show concentration across all 15
   participating counties.
4. Use latitude and longitude to map the records. What geographic patterns are
   visible, and what additional data would be needed before making claims about
   access or unmet need?
5. Investigate repeated addresses and similar business names. Propose a
   transparent entity-resolution rule, then explain how the result changes the
   number of apparent facilities without confusing provider records with
   facility-license identifiers.
6. The source is a current administrative list rather than a random sample or
   experiment. Which descriptive conclusions are supported, and which causal or
   statewide-access conclusions would be inappropriate?
